1.title: Why Friendships Fade

lines.text: Welcome back to Social Animals. Today we're looking at something almost everyone has experienced but rarely talks about: friendships that just, well, fizzle out. Dev, you've been reading up on this.
I have. And the first thing that struck me is how few friendships end with a dramatic falling-out. Most of them simply drift apart. Nobody breaks anything off; people just stop keeping up.
That rings true. I can think of three or four friends from university I was incredibly close to, and now we barely catch up once a year.

And the research suggests that's completely normal. One study found we replace about half our close friends every seven years. Life moves on. People move away, settle down, have kids, take up new jobs.
So is it something we should worry about?

Not necessarily. Some friendships are tied to a particular stage of life, and when that stage ends, they wind down naturally. The problem is when we let go of friendships we actually value, just because we never got round to calling.
Right. And there's that awkwardness, isn't there? The longer you leave it, the harder it is to pick up the phone.
Exactly. People assume the other person has moved on, or that they'll come across as needy. In fact, studies show people consistently underestimate how pleased friends are to hear from them.
That's quite reassuring. What about friendships that end badly? The genuine fallings-out?
Those are different. Usually, there's been a build-up. Someone feels let down, they don't bring it up, and it festers. Then one small thing sets it off.
And can those be patched up?
Often, yes, if both sides are willing to open up. It sometimes takes years, though. People need time to get over the hurt before they can bury the hatchet.
I'll admit, I've got one friendship like that. We fell out over a holiday, of all things. It's been five years.
Have you thought about reaching out?
I have, but, um, I keep putting it off. I suppose I'm worried she'll turn me down.
Well, the evidence suggests she probably won't. And even if she does, you'll have tried.
Fair point. OK, listeners, if you've reconnected with an old friend, or if you've decided to let a friendship go, we'd love to hear from you.
And Hannah, I'll be asking next week whether you've sent that message.
No pressure, then. Thanks, Dev.

1.title: Fifteen Years of Silence

lines.text: My guest today, Teresa Molina, didn't speak to her closest friend for fifteen years. Last spring, they reconciled. Teresa, thank you for agreeing to share this.
Thank you. I hesitated about doing it, to be honest, but I've come to think it might help someone.
Let's go back to the beginning. How did you meet?

We struck up a friendship on the first day of secondary school. I remember noticing her because she was the only other girl reading on the bus. We hit it off immediately. We were completely on the same wavelength.
And what went wrong?
She got married when we were twenty-six, and I'd promised to give a speech. The night before, I panicked and, well, I decided not to go. I told her I was ill. I wasn't.
That's quite a confession.
It is. I regret lying to her more than anything I've ever done. She found out a few weeks later, and she simply stopped answering my calls. I tried phoning for a while, and then I stopped trying.
Why did you stop?
Pride, mainly. I kept telling myself she'd overreacted. I didn't want to admit I'd let her down. I'd sooner have argued that I was right than apologised.
So what changed?
My mother died two years ago, and at the funeral, I found myself looking round for her. That was when I realised I'd never stopped missing her.
How did you get back in touch?

I wrote a letter. A real one, on paper. I remember spending three weekends trying to get the wording right. In the end I just stopped trying to justify myself and wrote, "I'm sorry. I was a coward, and I've regretted it every day."
And she answered?
Not for two months. I'd almost given up hoping. Then one morning she called. She said she'd meant to write back many times but couldn't bring herself to do it.
What was it like meeting again?
Awkward at first. We both tried to avoid mentioning the wedding. But then she stopped to look at me and said, "You still read on the bus, don't you?" And we both burst out laughing.
And now?
We meet every Sunday. It's not the same as before, it can't be, but it's grown into something maybe deeper.
Any advice for listeners in a similar situation?
Don't wait for a funeral. And when you apologise, don't explain. Just apologise.

2.title: Dressing the Characters

lines.text: My guest today is Ruth Adebayo, a costume designer who's worked on more than forty stage productions. Ruth, what does a costume designer actually do?
In a nutshell, I help the audience understand who a character is before they've said a word. Clothes do an enormous amount of storytelling.
Where do you start?

With the script, always. I read it three or four times, and I try to imagine what each character would choose to wear, which is not necessarily what looks best. Then I sit down with the director, who usually wants me to explain every decision.
Can you give me an example of a decision like that?

Sure. In a production of a Chekhov play last year, the director wanted the young heroine to wear white throughout. I persuaded her to let me dress her in hand-me-downs instead, slightly too big, slightly faded. It made the audience feel she was living in someone else's life.
That's a lovely detail. How do actors react to their costumes?

It varies enormously. Some actors refuse to rehearse until they've got the shoes. Shoes make you walk differently, and that changes everything. Others, er, would happily perform in their own jeans if I let them.
Do you ever have disagreements?

Of course. I once had an actor who insisted on wearing a very expensive designer suit for a character who was supposed to be broke. I had to convince him that it would undermine the whole performance.
How did you manage it?
I made him try on both and look in the mirror. The cheap suit made him stand differently. He ended up thanking me.
What about historical productions? How accurate do you have to be?

Less than people think. I tend to avoid being slavishly accurate. Audiences expect a character to look the part, but they need to recognise the signals. A completely accurate eighteenth-century outfit can look ridiculous to a modern eye.
You must spend a lot of time shopping.
Ha, yes. I love rummaging through second-hand markets. You can't fake the way fabric wears with age. I've learned to trust my instincts there.
Is there a costume you're most proud of?

Probably a dress I made for a woman playing a queen who'd lost everything. Understated, almost plain, but in a fabric that caught the light whenever she moved. It managed to suggest power and loss at the same time.
And what would you advise someone wanting to get into the profession?
Learn to sew properly. It sounds old-fashioned, but it lets you talk to the people making your costumes on equal terms. And go to the theatre constantly.

2.title: The Twenty-Pound Gala Challenge

lines.text: Welcome to Worn Well. This week, Marcus and I set ourselves a challenge. We each had twenty pounds and two hours in charity shops to put together an outfit for a black-tie gala. Marcus, you go first. What did you find?

Well, what I was most worried about was the jacket. Men's evening jackets are either enormous or tiny. But what happened was, in the third shop, I found a midnight-blue velvet dinner jacket for eight pounds.
Eight pounds! And did it fit?
Almost. The sleeves were a bit long. What I did was fold them under and pin them, which, er, is not a long-term solution.
And the rest?
A white shirt for three pounds, black trousers for five, and a bow tie I borrowed from my granddad. So, technically sixteen pounds.
Very impressive. How did people react at the gala?
What surprised me was that nobody guessed. Someone actually asked me which designer it was. I said "Oxfam" and she thought I was joking.
Ha! That's the thing, isn't it? People do judge a book by its cover. If you look the part, nobody asks questions.
Exactly. And what I've realised is that velvet is a cheat. It looks expensive, whatever it cost. Anyway, your turn. Were you dressed to the nines?
Hmm. Let's say I tried. What I wanted was something timeless, a long black dress. What I found was a lot of sequins from about 1987.
Oh no.

It's fine. In the end, I went for a plain navy silk dress for eleven pounds. It was a bit dull on its own, so what I did was add a vintage brooch and some long gloves. Very understated elegance. Or so I told myself.
It looked fantastic, honestly. What made it work was the gloves. Not many people could pull those off.
Thank you. But what I didn't plan for was the shoes. I had nothing under nine pounds, so I wore my own. Which is cheating, I admit.
We'll let it go. So, lessons for listeners?
For me, it's that what matters isn't the label but the fit. A cheap dress that fits beats an expensive one that doesn't.
And for me, it's go to charity shops in wealthy areas. That's where the good stuff ends up.
A bit cynical, but true. Next week, we're dressing down: a whole office wardrobe from hand-me-downs. Thanks for listening.

3.title: How the Fridge Changed Dinner
3.topic: Scientific advances and attitudes toward technology

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at a technology most of us take completely for granted: the refrigerator. It's not glamorous, but it's arguably one of the most important inventions of the twentieth century.
Before refrigeration, keeping food fresh was a constant struggle. In cities, people relied on ice, which was cut from frozen lakes in winter and stored in ice houses insulated with sawdust.
The ice was then delivered to homes by an iceman, who'd come round once or twice a week.

Now, the first practical refrigerators for the home appeared in the 1910s and 1920s. They were expensive, noisy and, in some cases, dangerous, because the early models used toxic gases. A leak could, and occasionally did, kill a family in their sleep.
Sorry, so how did they become safe?
Good question. The breakthrough came in the late 1920s with a new, non-toxic refrigerant. It made the fridge safe, cheap to produce and, crucially, something the average family could afford.
By the 1950s, the majority of American households owned one.
And this is where it gets interesting, because the fridge didn't just preserve food. It changed the way people shopped, cooked and even lived.
Think about shopping. Without a fridge, you bought milk and meat daily. With one, a single weekly trip became possible, which, in turn, helped create the supermarket.
And the supermarket helped create the suburb, because people needed cars to carry a week's shopping home.
So the fridge is partly responsible for the suburbs?
That's a slight exaggeration, but it's part of the story. Technologies rarely act alone. The car, the fridge and the supermarket grew up together.
Then there's diet. Fresh fruit and vegetables could be transported long distances. Frozen food arrived. The ready meal arrived. In many ways, the modern diet is a product of the cold chain.

Of course, there were unintended consequences. The chemicals that made fridges safe turned out to damage the ozone layer. That was only discovered in the 1970s, and those gases were finally phased out after an international agreement in 1987.
And today? Are fridges still a problem for the environment?

Less so, but they use a lot of electricity, and the cold chain as a whole has a significant carbon footprint. Researchers are now working on cutting-edge cooling systems that use magnets instead of gas.
Whether they'll render the current technology obsolete remains to be seen.
For next week, please read the chapter on the history of air conditioning, which tells a remarkably similar story.

3.title: Blood by Drone
3.topic: Scientific advances and attitudes toward technology

lines.text: Now, a story from the Scottish Highlands, where a hospital has begun using drones to deliver blood and medicines to remote clinics. Grace Allan reports.

Flying at about a hundred kilometres an hour, the small white drone takes just twenty minutes to cross the hills between Inverness and a clinic that used to be ninety minutes away by road. Having been loaded with two units of blood, it's launched from the hospital roof, and it lands on a marked square in the clinic car park.
The service has been running for three months. Dr Kwame Mensah, who leads the project, says it's already a game-changer.
Absolutely. Before this, if a patient needed blood urgently at one of our rural clinics, we'd send a car. In winter, with snow on the roads, that could take hours.
Now, having received the request, we can have blood there in less than half an hour.
The drones are flown automatically, following routes programmed in advance, but each flight is monitored by a pilot sitting at a screen in the hospital.
So far, the system has completed more than four hundred deliveries. Only two flights have been cancelled, both because of high winds.
Grace, what about safety? Hasn't there been some concern locally?
There has.

Some residents, worried about noise and privacy, objected when the trial was first announced. The hospital says the drones carry no cameras pointing at the ground, and they fly above a hundred and twenty metres, which keeps the noise to a minimum.
Not everyone is convinced, though. Speaking at a public meeting last week, a local farmer said that the drones were frightening his sheep. The hospital has agreed to adjust the routes.
Look, there are drawbacks to any new technology.
We're listening. But weighing up a few nervous sheep against a patient who might die waiting for blood, I think most people understand.

The question now is whether the system can be scaled. The NHS is considering rolling it out across other rural areas, but the cost is significant, about half a million pounds a year for this route alone.
Supporters argue that, having reduced the number of emergency ambulance journeys, the drones will pay for themselves within a few years. Critics say the money would be better spent on staff.
And the patients themselves?
Those I spoke to were overwhelmingly positive. One woman, having needed a transfusion after an accident in January, told me she simply wouldn't be here without it.
Grace Allan, thank you.

4.title: The Ghost of Room Fourteen

lines.text: For years, the Black Swan Inn in Yorkshire has claimed to be one of the most haunted hotels in England.
This week, its owner made a surprising announcement. Amira Khan reports.

Room fourteen of the Black Swan has a waiting list of nearly a year. Guests pay double the normal rate to sleep there, hoping to meet the so-called Grey Lady, a servant who, according to legend, died in the room in 1790.
But on Monday, the owner, Peter Ford, admitted that the ghost had been, in his words, "a bit of a family invention". I asked him to explain.
Well, my father bought the place in the seventies, and it was struggling. He told a journalist the story of the Grey Lady, and, er, the next week we were fully booked.
He never actually claimed to have seen her. He just never denied it.
Mr Ford insists that he didn't set out to deceive anyone. He says he decided to come clean after a guest complained that the ghost hadn't appeared and demanded a refund.
That was the moment I thought, this has gone too far. People were taking it at face value. Some guests were genuinely frightened.

Not everyone has welcomed his confession. Local historian Margaret Lowe, who has researched the inn, pointed out that there really was a servant who died there in 1790, although there's no evidence that she ever haunted anyone.
Mrs Lowe also suggested that Mr Ford's announcement might itself be a publicity stunt. Mr Ford denied this, and assured me that bookings had actually fallen since Monday.
Meanwhile, some regular guests have refused to accept the confession. One woman, who has stayed in room fourteen six times, insisted that she had heard footsteps every single time.
She accused Mr Ford of "betraying the Grey Lady".
I can't tell people what they did or didn't experience. Old buildings make noises.
Pipes, wood, the wind. People hear what they want to hear.
A paranormal society in Leeds has urged the owner to let them carry out an investigation before the story is finally closed. Mr Ford has agreed, although he warned them not to expect much.
And what about room fourteen? Mr Ford has promised to keep it open, but he's lowered the price.
The ghost, he joked, has been "demoted to standard rate".
Amira Khan reporting.

lines.text: OK, let's begin. This week's topic is superstition in professional sport. Tom, you've been looking at football. What did you find?
Well, superstitions are said to be extremely common among footballers. One survey suggests that around eighty per cent of professional players have at least one pre-match ritual.
What kind of rituals?
All sorts. Some players are known to put their left boot on before their right, every single time. One famous goalkeeper is reported to have worn the same unwashed shirt for an entire season.
Ugh. Was that true, or just a story?
Fair question. It's widely claimed, but I couldn't find a reliable source. A lot of this is anecdotal, which is a bit of a problem.

That's a really important point. Much of what is said about sporting superstitions comes from interviews and memoirs rather than systematic research. We should be careful not to lend too much credence to individual stories. Aisha, what about the research side?

So, there actually is some interesting research. Superstitions are thought to reduce anxiety. When an outcome is uncertain and partly outside your control, a ritual is believed to give you a sense of control.
Is there any evidence that they improve performance?
There was a well-known study in 2010 where golfers were told they'd been given a "lucky ball". They were found to putt significantly better than golfers using an ordinary ball.
Seriously? That sounds a bit far-fetched.
I thought so too. And actually, when other researchers tried to repeat it, they couldn't reproduce the result. So the original finding has been largely debunked, or at least seriously questioned.
That's a classic replication problem. So where does that leave us?
I'd say it is generally accepted that rituals reduce stress. Whether they improve results is much less clear.
There's also the risk side. A player whose ritual is interrupted, say, because they forgot their lucky socks, is said to perform worse because they're anxious about it.
Interesting. So the superstition creates the problem it claims to solve.
Exactly. And coaches are increasingly reported to be replacing superstitions with routines, things like breathing exercises, that have the same calming effect without the dependency.
Good. For next week, I'd like each of you to find one claim about superstition that's attributed to "research" in the media, and track down the original study. Let's see how many survive.

lines.text: My guest today has been set on fire, thrown through windows and dropped off buildings, all professionally. Jack Moran has been a stunt performer for eighteen years. Jack, welcome.
Thanks. It sounds much more dramatic when you list it like that.
How did you get into it?

By accident, really. I was a gymnast, and I was so bored after giving up competition that I answered an advert for extras on an action film. The stunt coordinator saw me fall off a horse, quite badly, actually, and offered me a job.
Falling off a horse got you a job?
It was such a good fall that he assumed I'd done it on purpose. I didn't correct him.
What's the most dangerous stunt you've done?
Probably a car going off a bridge into a river. The water was so cold that my hands stopped working after about thirty seconds. And you're inside a sinking car, so, er, you really need your hands.
That's terrifying.
It was. But the preparation was so thorough that I never felt in real danger. We rehearsed it twenty times in a pool first. There were four divers in the water.
Do audiences realise how much planning goes into these scenes?
Not really, and that's sort of the point. If a stunt is done well, it looks so natural that nobody thinks about it. The best stunts are the ones you don't notice.
Have you been injured?
Plenty of times. Broken ribs, a shoulder, a fractured ankle. The ankle was such a stupid accident. I tripped over a cable walking to lunch.
After eighteen years of jumping off buildings.
Exactly. My mum still laughs about it.
How has the industry changed?

Hugely. These days so much is done digitally that people assume stunts are disappearing. They're not. Directors still want real bodies doing real things, because audiences can feel the difference, even if they can't explain it.
And safety?
It's so much better than when I started. There used to be a culture where if you complained, someone else would happily take your job. That's changing, although slowly.
Is there a stunt you still want to do?
A high fall, from about thirty metres, onto an airbag. I've done twenty-five. The fear is such a strange feeling at that height that you have to sort of switch your brain off.
And when will you stop?
When my body tells me to. It's already sending, er, polite emails.

6.title: Why We Can't Stop Humming
6.topic: Musical tastes, artists and defining success

lines.text: Good morning. Today's topic is one you've all experienced: the earworm, that song you can't get out of your head. And, more broadly, the question of why some songs become hits and others fade into obscurity.
Let's start with a simple principle known as the mere exposure effect. Basically, the more often we hear something, the more we tend to like it. Up to a point.
Up to what point?

Good question. Studies suggest that liking increases with repetition and then, after a certain number of plays, starts to decline. So the curve looks like an upside-down U. The catchier a song is, the faster you reach the top of that curve, and, unfortunately, the faster you get tired of it.
That partly explains the one-hit wonder. A song that's extremely catchy can go viral, but the very quality that makes it spread also makes people sick of it more quickly.
So songs that grow on you slowly last longer?
Broadly, yes. Research on chart data suggests that songs which climb the charts slowly tend to stay there longer. The slower the rise, the longer the stay, roughly speaking.

Now, what makes a song catchy in the first place? One large study of earworms found a few common features. A fairly fast tempo, a melody that's simple to sing, and an unusual interval or leap somewhere in the tune. Something slightly surprising.
So it's a balance. The more predictable a melody is, the easier it is to remember, but the more boring it becomes. Too much surprise, though, and it becomes hard to follow.
What about lyrics? Do they matter?
They matter for emotion more than memory. A lyric that strikes a chord with people's experience makes a song feel personal. But people often remember the melody and get the words completely wrong.
That's definitely me.

You're not alone. Now, why do some songs stand the test of time? This is harder. Partly, it's that they become attached to memories. The older we get, the more we value the music of our teenage years.
And there's a cultural effect. The more a song is used in films, adverts, weddings, the more it becomes part of shared memory. It's a self-reinforcing loop.
Isn't that a bit depressing? It sounds like quality doesn't matter.
It matters, but it's not sufficient. Plenty of brilliant songs are forgotten, and plenty of derivative ones are hits. Luck and timing play a huge role.
For next week, I'd like you to keep an earworm diary. Every time a song gets stuck in your head, note what it was and what you were doing. We'll compare results.
What if it's always the same song?
Then the harder you try to stop it, the worse it'll get. That's another finding, I'm afraid.

6.title: Life After the Hit
6.topic: Musical tastes, artists and defining success

lines.text: People still stop me in the supermarket, you know. They'll look at me for a few seconds, and then they'll start humming. Always the chorus. Never the verses.

For anyone who doesn't know, I was the singer in a band called The Paper Kites. We had one hit, in 1998. "Summer Static". It went to number two, and it stayed in the charts for eleven weeks. So yes, I'm a one-hit wonder. I've made my peace with that.

When we were starting out, we'd rehearse in my parents' garage every evening. My dad would bang on the door at ten o'clock exactly, and shout, "That's enough noise for one night!" Every single night, for three years.
We'd play anywhere. Pubs, weddings, a school fete once, which was a disaster. And we'd write constantly. Most of it was rubbish, honestly. Derivative stuff. We'd copy whoever was big that month.
Then one night, our bass player came in with this riff, and the song took about an hour to write. I remember thinking, that's quite catchy. That was it. No big moment.
Six months later, we were on television. And for about a year, everything was mad. Hotels, interviews, people screaming. I'd wake up and not know which country I was in.
The second album sold almost nothing. The record company would ring every week, asking for "another Summer Static". But you can't do that on purpose. If you try, it sounds like a cheap copy.
By 2002, the band had split up, and I'd, er, I'd lost a lot of money. I won't pretend that part was easy.
These days, I teach guitar to teenagers. And I love it, honestly. Some of them have no idea who I am, which is quite refreshing.

I'll still play the song sometimes, at a wedding or a charity gig. And the funny thing is, people's faces change. The song strikes a chord, not because it's brilliant, but because it reminds them of being seventeen.
My students will sometimes find the video online and laugh at my hair. Fair enough. It was very big hair.
Do I wish we'd had more hits? Of course. But lots of bands never have one. Ours has stood the test of time better than anyone expected.
And it still pays for the occasional holiday. So, you know, I'll keep humming along with the people in the supermarket.
My dad, by the way, is eighty-one now. And he'll still tell anyone who'll listen that the song was written in his garage.
He'll leave out the part about banging on the door, of course.
Every time he tells the story, the garage gets a bit bigger. Last time, it had a stage.
That's the thing about a hit. Everyone wants a piece of it, even your dad.
Anyway. Time for my next lesson.

7.title: Learning to Drive, Then and Now

lines.text: For generations, passing the driving test was the rite of passage that marked the end of childhood. But fewer young people are now learning to drive. Sam Okoro has been finding out why.

In 1990, around eighty per cent of British people aged twenty to twenty-nine held a driving licence. Today, the figure is closer to sixty per cent. The reasons people give are varied, but the one that comes up most is cost.
I went to meet Bev Harris, who has been a driving instructor in Bristol for thirty-four years, and whose own instructor, she tells me, was her uncle.
My uncle taught me in a Ford Escort that he'd bought from a neighbour. It had a gearbox you had to fight with. The lessons he gave me cost nothing, apart from patience.
And the lessons you give now?
Around forty pounds an hour. Most learners need about forty-five hours. Then there's insurance, which for a seventeen-year-old can be two or three thousand pounds a year.
It adds up to a figure that a lot of families just can't afford.
But it isn't only money. For many young people I spoke to, the car simply doesn't mean what it meant to their parents.

One nineteen-year-old I met, who lives in central Bristol, told me the freedom his dad found in a car, he finds in his phone and a bus pass. The friends he wants to see are, as he put it, "one message away".
That's the generation gap in a nutshell. When I was young, the car was the thing that let you escape. You'd look back on your first drive alone as a milestone.
These days, I get learners whose parents have booked the lessons, and who'd honestly rather be somewhere else.
Others, though, still see it as formative. A student I spoke to, whose family lives in a village with two buses a day, said passing her test last month was "the biggest moment of my life so far".
And there are regional differences. In rural areas, where public transport is limited, the proportion of young drivers has fallen much less.
With hindsight, I think we made the car too central. Whole towns were built around it. So the young people who live in those places don't really have a choice.
Is there any nostalgia, I asked her, for the old days?

For the cars, a little. For the roads, no. There was a lot of bad driving that nobody did anything about. The test I took in 1985 lasted twenty minutes. Today's is far more demanding, and that's a good thing.
So, is the driving test still a rite of passage? For some, clearly. But for a growing number, the milestone that matters is something else entirely.
Sam Okoro reporting.

lines.text: Pass me that album, Leo. The green one. I want to show you something.

Is this you? You look as though you're about to burst into tears.
Ha. I probably was. That was my first day at school, 1958. My mother made me wear shoes that were two sizes too big, so I'd grow into them.
That's brutal.
That was the way things were done. Nothing was wasted. Look at this one, my brother's eighteenth birthday. We had cake and lemonade in the kitchen, and the whole street came.
It looks like a film set. Everyone's smiling like they've been told to.
They had been told to! My father would stand there with the camera and say, "Nobody moves until I say so." It took forever.
And who's this? He looks as if he owns the place.
That's your grandfather, the summer we met. He did act like he owned the place, to be fair. He was very confident.
You're blushing, Grandma.

That sounds terrifying. Mum won't let me ride in the front till I'm twelve.
I know. Sometimes I feel as if I grew up on another planet. But I'm not one of those people who say everything was better. It wasn't. A lot of it was harder.

People talked more, I think. We didn't have a screen to look at, so we looked at each other. That's the thing I hark back to, not the shoes.
You talk as though phones are evil.
No, no. I video-call your aunt in Chicago every week. Thirty years ago, it would have cost a fortune. I'm just saying, the way you young people live, you sometimes miss what's right in front of you.

9.title: On the Trail of the Spectacled Bear
9.topic: Animals, ethics and the natural world

lines.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the reserve. Before we set off, a few ground rules. Whenever you hear me whistle twice, please stop and stay completely still. It usually means I've spotted something.
Will we actually see a bear?
Honestly? Probably not. Spectacled bears are incredibly shy. But wherever they've been, they leave signs, and I'll show you how to read them.
OK, let's go. Stay on the path wherever possible. The cloud forest is a fragile ecosystem, and every footstep off the trail damages plants that took decades to grow.
Why is it called a spectacled bear?
Because of the pale markings around its eyes. They look a bit like glasses. And every bear's markings are unique, like fingerprints. That's how researchers identify individuals.
Right, look here. See these bromeliads, these spiky plants, torn open on the ground? A bear's been feeding. They pull them apart to get at the soft centre. This was recent, maybe yesterday.
How many bears live in the reserve?
We think around thirty. When I started working here, fifteen years ago, it was fewer than twenty. So conservation is working, slowly.
What's the biggest threat to them?

Habitat loss, mostly. Farms keep encroaching on the forest, and wherever a road is built, bears end up in conflict with people. Some farmers shoot them when they eat their maize. And poaching still happens, though it's much rarer now.
We work with the farmers rather than against them. Whenever a bear damages a crop, the reserve pays compensation. It's not perfect, but it's reduced the killings dramatically.
That seems fair.
It's the only thing that works. If people lose money whenever a bear appears, the bear will lose.
OK, stop for a moment. Look up, in that tree. See the platform of broken branches? That's a bear nest. They build them to rest in during the day.
In a tree? I had no idea bears climbed that high.
They're excellent climbers. Wherever there's fruit, they'll find a way up.

Now, the species isn't on the brink of extinction, but it's classified as vulnerable. Its resilience depends on whether we can keep the forest connected. Bears need to move between valleys to find mates.
We're coming to the viewpoint now. Whenever the clouds lift, you can see all three valleys from here. Cameras ready.
It's beautiful.
It is. And with luck, it'll still look like this when your grandchildren come.

9.title: Can You Buy Your Way to Green?
9.topic: Animals, ethics and the natural world

lines.text: Good evening. Tonight's question: carbon offsetting. Is paying to plant trees or protect forests a genuine solution, or a way for polluters to feel better? Dr Mwangi, you work on conservation projects in Kenya. You're broadly in favour?

With conditions, yes. Whatever you think of the concept, offset money is currently funding real conservation. In the project I work on, it pays for rangers, it stops poaching, and it gives local communities an income that doesn't depend on cutting down forest.

Can I come in? Nobody's denying that some projects do good work. My concern is that offsets let whoever is doing the polluting carry on exactly as before. An airline can sell you a "carbon-neutral" flight, and nothing about the flight has changed.
That's true, but the alternative isn't that the flight disappears. People will fly anyway. Surely it's better that whoever flies pays something towards protecting an ecosystem.
It's better than nothing, maybe. But "better than nothing" isn't a climate policy. And whatever the marketing says, a tree planted today won't absorb that carbon for decades, if it survives at all.
Dr Mwangi, how do you respond to the point about survival?
It's a fair one. Badly managed planting schemes have been a real problem. Whoever designed some of those projects didn't consult local people, and the trees died within a couple of years.
That's why I'm in favour of protecting existing forests rather than planting new ones.
Even then, there's the question of whether the forest was ever actually under threat. Some studies have found that many protected areas would have survived anyway.
So the offset isn't stopping anything. It's just, um, paying for something that was going to happen.
In some cases, yes. That's why verification is crucial. But I'd reject the idea that we should throw the whole system out. Biodiversity in our region has recovered noticeably since the funding began.
Ms Carter, is there a version of offsetting you'd support?

Possibly. If it came after serious cuts, not instead of them. Whichever company wants to call itself green should first show it has reduced its own emissions. Then offsets can deal with whatever is genuinely impossible to cut.
I'd actually agree with that. Offsetting should be the last step, not the first.
So there's more common ground than I expected. What should the public do?
Be sceptical of whatever label says "carbon neutral". Ask what's been reduced first.
And if you do pay for an offset, find out who runs the project and whether local communities benefit. Whoever is on the ground should have a say.
Thank you both.

10.title: How a Word Gets into the Dictionary
10.topic: Effective communication and attitudes toward language

lines.text: Good morning. A question I'm often asked is, "Who decides which words go into the dictionary?" The honest answer is that nobody decides, at least not in the way people imagine. Words are collected, not invented by lexicographers.
Let me explain the process. For a major English dictionary, new words are tracked in an enormous database of real language, what we call a corpus.
It's made up of billions of words that have been taken from books, newspapers, websites, transcripts of speech.
When a new word appears, it's flagged automatically. But a single appearance isn't enough. A word has to be used by a lot of different people, in different places, over a period of several years.
If it's only used by one group, or for one summer, it's usually ignored.
So slang words that go viral for a few months don't get in?
Generally not. Many of them are monitored, but they're never added, because they've disappeared by the time the editors look again. Others have been on the list for a decade before being accepted.

Once a word has been judged stable enough, a definition is drafted. That's harder than it sounds. The editor has to look at hundreds of examples and work out what the word actually means in use, which isn't always what people think it means.
The draft is then checked by other editors, and in specialist areas, like medicine or law, it's sent to outside experts. Each entry may be revised several times before it's published.
How long does all that take?
For a straightforward word, months. For a complicated one, years. And remember that existing entries are being updated all the time, too.
Words change meaning. "Awful" used to mean "full of awe". The entry for it has been rewritten more than once.

Now, some people believe that, once a word has been included, it's been officially approved as correct English. That's a misunderstanding. The dictionary describes how the language is used; it doesn't tell you how it should be used.
So if enough people use a word wrongly, does it become right?

That's the big question, isn't it? From the dictionary's point of view, yes, eventually. "Decimate" originally meant to kill one in ten. Today it's used to mean "destroy most of", and that meaning has been recorded for over a century.

Interestingly, more and more loan words are being added. English has always borrowed. Words have been taken from Hindi, Arabic, Spanish, Japanese. In the last update alone, dozens of words from other languages were included.

Finally, will dictionaries still be needed in twenty years? I'd say yes, though they'll be consulted on screens, not shelves. And the corpus will probably have been expanded to include far more spoken language.
For next week, I'd like each of you to find a word that's been added in the last five years and track its first recorded use. You'll be surprised how old some "new" words are.

10.title: Raising Children in Three Languages
10.topic: Effective communication and attitudes toward language

lines.text: Welcome to Mother Tongues. My guest today is Yusuf, who lives in Toronto with his wife and two kids, and the family speaks three languages at home. Yusuf, how does that work?

Chaotically, at times. So, I'm from Turkey, my wife's from Brazil, and we live in Canada. I speak Turkish to the children, my wife speaks Portuguese, and between ourselves we speak English. Each of us sticks to our own language with the kids. That's the rule.
And does it work?
Mostly. Both of our children understand all three. But neither of them speaks Turkish as well as I'd like. English is everywhere, so it's always winning.
That's common, isn't it?

Very. A number of families we know have given up on the third language completely. The number of hours you need is huge. Every one of the experts we talked to said the same thing: if a language isn't used outside the home, it's hard to keep it alive.
So what do you do about Turkish?

We go to Istanbul every summer. Two months. And none of my relatives speaks English, which is perfect. After a week, the kids have no choice. By August, my daughter is chatting away and picking up slang I've never heard.
Do the children ever mix the languages?

All the time. My son will start a sentence in English, use a Portuguese word in the middle, and finish in Turkish. People used to think that was a sign of confusion. Actually, most of the research suggests it's the opposite. He's choosing whatever word gets his point across fastest.
What's been the hardest part?

Honestly? Feeling like the odd one out. My wife and the kids share a lot of Brazilian culture, music, food. Turkish feels like my thing alone. And there's a bit of grief, sometimes, when my son replies in English to something I've said in Turkish.
That sounds painful.
It is, a little. But the majority of my friends who grew up bilingual say the same thing: they resisted as teenagers and were grateful as adults. So I'm playing a long game.
Any advice for listeners in the same situation?

Be consistent, but don't be strict. Some parents punish children for answering in the wrong language, and the result is that the child hates the language. Make it fun. Songs, cartoons, cooking. And get the grandparents involved. Each grandparent is worth about ten hours of lessons.
Yusuf, thank you.
Thank you. Or, er, teşekkürler. Obrigado.

11.title: The Mechanic Who Built a Hand
11.topic: Role models, values and high achievers

lines.text: Tonight, the story of a self-taught engineer whose low-cost prosthetic hands are changing lives across Central America. Lena Brooks reports from Guatemala.
In a small, brightly lit workshop on the edge of Quetzaltenango, a twenty-eight-year-old mechanic is fitting a 3D-printed hand onto the arm of a nine-year-old girl.
She closes her new fingers around a plastic cup and lifts it. Her mother starts crying.
Mateo Ruiz never went to university. He left school at fifteen to work in his uncle's car-repair shop. But he's become one of the best-known names in low-cost prosthetics in the region.
It started with my cousin. He lost his hand in a farm accident, and a prosthetic from the city cost more than his family earned in two years. I thought, I fix engines all day. How hard can a hand be?
Very hard, it turned out. Mateo spent two years teaching himself design software from online videos, often working through the night after long, back-breaking shifts at the garage.
My first hand was terrible. Heavy, ugly, and it broke after a week. My cousin was very kind about it. He said it was "a good-looking disaster".

But Mateo kept going. His current design, a lightweight, easy-to-repair model, costs about eighty dollars to make, compared with several thousand for a commercial device. It's fully open-source, so anyone with a 3D printer can download and build it.

So far, the workshop has fitted more than six hundred hands, mostly to children. Because children grow, they need a new hand every year or so, which makes expensive devices almost impossible for poor families.
For children, a cheap hand is better than an expensive one. When they grow out of it, we make a bigger one. Free.
Not everyone is convinced. A doctor I spoke to warned that some home-made devices are poorly fitted and can cause long-term problems.
Mateo agrees that quality control is essential and now works with a local physiotherapist, who checks every fitting.
His story has made him something of a role model.

Young people from across the country write to him asking how to start. Last year, he was invited to speak at a conference in Mexico City, alongside some of the most highly qualified engineers in the field.
I was nervous. They all had PhDs. I had grease under my fingernails. But they listened. Good ideas don't need a certificate.
Mateo's next goal is a hand with simple electronic sensors, at a price families can afford. He's confident he'll get there.
Back in the workshop, the nine-year-old is now trying to pick up a pencil. On the third attempt, she manages it, and the whole room cheers.
Lena Brooks reporting.

11.title: Choosing the Teacher of the Year
11.topic: Role models, values and high achievers

lines.text: Right, we've narrowed it down to two finalists for Teacher of the Year. We need a decision by five o'clock. Peter, make your case for Mr Lewis.

Happily. Frank Lewis is, without question, the longest-serving teacher on our list. Forty-one years at the same school. He's taught the parents of half his current students. Several former pupils described him as the most inspiring person they've ever met.
No one disputes that. But I'd argue Ms Okafor's achievements are more far-reaching.
Go on, Asha.

Grace Okafor is only twenty-nine, but she's already one of the most innovative, forward-thinking teachers I've come across. She took over the worst-performing science department in the district and, in three years, it's become one of the best-performing. Against all odds, honestly. The school was close to being closed.

That's impressive. But results aren't everything. Frank is the kindest, most patient man I know. Students who were written off by other teachers have done remarkable things because he refused to give up on them.

I don't doubt it. But Grace has done that on a larger scale. She set up a free after-school club, which has become the best-attended programme in the school. And she's trained other teachers in her methods. That's a legacy that will outlast her.
With respect, Frank's legacy already has. Forty years of students. One of them is now a surgeon who credits him with her whole career.
Can I ask both of you: what is the award actually for? Lifetime achievement, or this year?
This year, according to the criteria. "Outstanding contribution in the past twelve months."
Hmm. That's, er, a fair point. Although I'd say Frank's contribution this year was as strong as ever. He's still the most hard-working member of staff, and he's in his sixties.
Nobody's questioning his dedication. I just think Grace is the most deserving candidate under these criteria. She's a trailblazer.
And Frank is a role model. The most widely respected teacher in the region.
OK. Here's a thought. The organisers mentioned that we can recommend a separate lifetime achievement award. What if Grace gets Teacher of the Year, and Frank gets that?
I'd be comfortable with that, as long as it's presented on the same night, not as an afterthought.
Agreed. He deserves a proper moment.
Good. That's settled. I'll write to the organisers this afternoon.
And Diane, make sure the speech is short. Frank hates fuss.
Noted.

12.title: Closing the Deal on Bamboo Bikes
12.topic: Entrepreneurship, negotiation and the ideal job

lines.text: Hello, Kofi? It's Anna from Green Wheel. Thanks for making time. I wanted to follow up on our quote before our board meets on Thursday.
Of course, Anna. Good to hear from you. Have you had a chance to look at the figures?
I have, and I'll be honest. The frames are beautiful, but the unit price is higher than we'd budgeted for. Were we to place a larger order, could you bring it down?
Possibly. What sort of volume are we talking about?
We'd been thinking of two hundred frames for the first season. Should the first batch sell well, we could go up to five hundred next year.
OK. Had you mentioned five hundred at the start, I'd have priced it differently. For two hundred, the best I can do is a five per cent discount. For five hundred, I could go to twelve.
Twelve's interesting. But we're a small company, and we're only just in the black. I can't commit to five hundred without knowing the first batch will sell.

I understand. What if we did this: you order two hundred now at the five per cent rate, and should you reorder within twelve months, I'll apply the twelve per cent retrospectively to the first order as well.
That's creative. I like it. Let me check one thing, though. Delivery. Our last supplier was three months late, and it nearly sank us.
Our lead time is ten weeks from the deposit. Should there be any delay on our side, we'd cover the cost of air freight. That's in the contract.
Good. And quality? We've done our due diligence, and your references are excellent. But were any frames to crack in the first year, what happens?
We replace them free of charge. To be fair, it's never happened yet. Bamboo is surprisingly strong.
I'm sure. OK, one last point. Payment terms. We'd prefer thirty per cent upfront and the rest on delivery, rather than fifty-fifty.
Hmm. That's tight for us. Our workshop is still scaling up. Could we meet in the middle? Forty per cent upfront?
Forty I can probably get past the board. Should they object, I'll call you on Friday.
Perfect. Then I'll draft the agreement tonight. Should you need anything else for Thursday, a sample frame, photos, anything, just say.
A sample frame would be brilliant, actually. The board likes to touch things.
I'll courier one tomorrow. And Anna, had you not called today, I was going to call you. We really want this partnership to get off the ground.
So do we. Speak soon, Kofi.

12.title: Pitch Night: The Rooftop Farm
12.topic: Entrepreneurship, negotiation and the ideal job

lines.text: Welcome to Founders' Corner. My guest, Jada Owens, pitched her company, Up Top Farms, to a panel of investors last night. Jada, first of all, how did it go?
Better than I expected, honestly. Two of the five investors made offers. But both came with conditions, so I haven't said yes to anyone yet.
Remind us what the business does.
We turn unused rooftops in the city into vegetable farms. Restaurants on the floors below buy the produce, so it travels about twenty metres instead of two hundred miles.
And the conditions?

The first investor offered two hundred thousand dollars, on condition that we focus only on restaurants and drop our community gardens. I'm not sure I can accept that. The community side is why I started.
And the second?
She offered less, a hundred and fifty, but she'd let us keep the community gardens provided that they break even within two years. That seems reasonable, as long as we can find sponsors.
Which way are you leaning?
The second, probably. Even if it means growing more slowly. Unless the first investor changes his mind, I'll most likely go with her.
What were the hardest questions on the night?

Revenue. They wanted to know how we'd make money in winter. We're in Chicago, so, er, rooftops are frozen for four months. I explained that we're installing greenhouses, but only if the building owners agree. Otherwise, we'd scale back production in winter and focus on selling seedlings.
Were you nervous?

Terrified. But I'd rehearsed so much. A mentor told me, "Assuming you get asked the worst possible question, what will you say?" So I prepared answers for twenty worst questions. In the end, they only asked three of them.
What would you tell someone preparing their first pitch?
Know your numbers better than anyone in the room. And don't accept money just because it's offered. Supposing the investor wants a completely different company, are you willing to run it?
And what happens if neither deal works out?
Then we carry on. We're not in the red. We could grow slowly from our own revenue, as long as we keep costs down. It would just take longer to get the bigger projects off the ground.
When do you have to decide?
By Friday. In case either of them withdraws, I've also kept talking to a bank. Just as a backup.
Jada, good luck with the decision.
Thanks, Rob. And if anyone listening owns an empty roof, you know where to find me.
